text: A real incident response plan isn't a binder written once to satisfy an auditor. It's a reference document the team actually opens while an incident is happening, often at 2 a.m., under stress, with normal tools half-unavailable. That single fact drives every design decision in a plan worth having.

A real plan starts with scope and objectives: what counts as an incident, and what the plan is trying to achieve. Then severity classification criteria, decided in advance on a defined scale like SEV1 through SEV4, so nobody debates the severity level while the clock is running. Then a communication plan spelling out exactly who gets notified, in what order, within what time window, for each severity level.

Three more components round it out. Escalation paths define the specific thresholds for moving a decision up the chain when the on-call responder doesn't have authority to make it alone. A tool and access inventory lists where to find credentials and out-of-band channels if the normal network is down or compromised. And legal and regulatory notification requirements flag the real deadlines: GDPR's 72-hour window, state breach-notification laws, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SEC disclosure rules.

Picture a ransomware note on a file server at 2 a.m. The analyst doesn't debate what to do. The plan's severity criteria already say ransomware with lateral movement is SEV1. The communication plan says SEV1 wakes the Incident Commander immediately, the CISO within 30 minutes, legal within an hour. The tool inventory points to an offline credential vault, since the compromised network's own password manager might be unreachable.

That last detail matters more than it sounds like it should. A plan stored only on the intranet wiki or the CISO's personal laptop is useless the moment the network goes down or that one person is unreachable. A plan that actually survives a bad night lives somewhere outside the systems it describes responding to: a printed binder, an offline vault, an out-of-band chat group the team can reach no matter what else is broken.

Get those six pieces right and the plan becomes something the team can execute under pressure instead of argue about. Next, Lesson 6 moves from the general plan to playbooks -- the specific, pre-thought-out response sequences for known scenario types like ransomware, business email compromise, data exfiltration, and insider threats.
